record.paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
record.original_question: For an n-vertex graph G and a specified pair of vertices, construct an exact counting algorithm running in O*(1.99^n) time that counts the number of paths between the two specified vertices, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: Count the number of paths between a given pair of vertices in G.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices, and let $s,t\in V$ be two distinguished vertices. A path from $s$ to $t$ is a sequence of distinct vertices $s=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k=t$ with $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}\in E$ for all $0\le i<k$. Let $P(G,s,t)$ denote the number of such paths.

For functions $f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{>0}$, write $f(n)=O^*(g(n))$ if there exists a polynomial $p$ such that $f(n)\le p(n)\,g(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$ (i.e., $O^*$ suppresses factors polynomial in $n$).

Design a deterministic exact algorithm that, given $G$ and the pair $(s,t)$, computes $P(G,s,t)$ in time $O^*(1.99^{n})$; equivalently, produce a constant $c<2$ and an algorithm computing $P(G,s,t)$ exactly in time $O^*(c^{n})$.
artifact.category_tag: Exact exponential algorithms for path counting
artifact.status_search_result: The standard inclusion–exclusion approach yields an $O^*(2^n)$ algorithm for counting $s$–$t$ paths in an $n$-vertex graph, and no algorithm breaking the $2^n$ barrier for exact counting of $s$–$t$ paths appears to be known in the literature. Recent works on $s$–$t$ simple path counting focus on practical pruning rather than worst-case exponential improvements, suggesting the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Effectively Counting s−t Simple Paths in Directed Graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Recent works address practical pruning techniques for counting s-t simple paths, without claiming sub-2^n worst-case bounds.
status_evidence.claim: No known sub-2^n exact algorithm for counting s-t paths is reported.

status_evidence.title: Hamiltonian path problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Björklund's Monte Carlo algorithm decides Hamiltonicity in O(1.657^n); counting variants remain harder and no analogous result is stated for counting s-t paths.
status_evidence.claim: Decision/Hamiltonicity improvements exist, but no corresponding sub-2^n bound is reported for counting s-t paths.
